info.name: AdPal API · Dual-Rail (Solana Devnet + PayPal Sandbox)
info.description:
Integration suite for the AdPal attention-billing simulator and its two settlement rails.

## What this exercises

| Rail | Credential | Settles |
|---|---|---|
| `paypal_payouts` | PayPal REST Sandbox | 70/30 split as a Payouts batch |
| `solana-devnet` | Solana Devnet | 70/30 split as one atomic transfer + memo |

The L402 protocol is the spine: a `402 Payment Required` challenge binds a `sha256(preimage)` invoice, the attention proof mints a macaroon, and the macaroon unlocks the paid resource. On the Solana rail the same 32-byte hash is anchored on-chain as a memo, so the invoice becomes publicly verifiable.

## Run order matters

Requests are ordered and chained through collection variables:

1. **Discovery** stores the active rail and the Solana wallet profile.
2. **L402** issues a challenge, then settles it. `payment_context_token` and `payment_hash` flow from the challenge into the settle body; `bearer_token` flows from settle into the unlock request.
3. **Solana verification** confirms on-chain signatures against the settled hash.
4. **Payouts** exercise both rails explicitly.

## Expected non-200 statuses

Three responses are intentionally not `200`:

- `GET /api/l402/offer` → **402**. This endpoint *is* the gated resource.
- `POST /api/l402/challenge` → **402**. A challenge is a refusal by definition.
- `POST /api/l402/solana/confirm` with a bad signature → **402**.

## Devnet funding

The Solana treasury needs devnet SOL to anchor proofs and move funds. When the public faucet is rate-limited, the rail degrades honestly instead of failing: the receipt records `anchor.status = "unfunded"`, and a Solana payout falls back to PayPal with an explicit `fallback` block. The tests accept both outcomes and assert the shape either way — a green run means "the server behaved correctly", not "the faucet was available".

Fund the treasury at `https://faucet.solana.com` using the `treasury` address from `GET /api/solana`.

item.name: 02 · L402 Protocol (402 → macaroon → 200)
item.description:
The full protocol handshake. The challenge's `payment_context_token` and `payment_hash` are stored and reused by the settle request; settle's `bearer_token` is reused by the unlock request.

Run these in order — each one feeds the next.

request.description:
Returns **402**, not 200: this endpoint is the paid resource. The body is the L402 contract — offer list, price, and a challenge binding a `sha256(preimage)` payment hash.

Present a `Bearer` macaroon (see the unlock request) to get 200 instead.

Explicitly starts a negotiation. Returns **402** with a new `payment_context_token` and the `payment_hash` the attention proof must commit to.

The token is stored for the settle request, so a single run chains end to end.

On success the ledger is credited 70/30, a macaroon is minted, and the settlement queues an automatic payout on the configured rail (`PAYOUT_RAIL`, currently `solana-devnet`).

item.name: 03 · Solana On-Chain Verification
item.description:
Re-reads a devnet transaction from the cluster and checks it against the settled invoice: confirmation status, memo binding to `sha256(preimage)`, recipient and exact base-unit amount.

The two rejection requests are deterministic and always run. The third only meaningful when the treasury is funded and an anchor signature exists.

// answer WrongSize, so it must be caught locally.
pm.test('names the format check as the failure', () => {
pm.test('echoes the signature and the invoice hash it was checked against', () => {

request.description: Sends 64 base58 characters that decode to only ~47 bytes. The route must reject this with **402** and a `format` check — never a 500 from the RPC's `WrongSize` error.

pm.test('still builds an explorer link for the attempted signature', () => {

request.description: A well-formed 64-byte signature that devnet has never seen. The route reads the cluster, finds nothing, and refuses with **402** — while still returning the checks array so the caller knows why.

request.description:
Confirms the anchor signature captured from the settle response: the transaction is re-read from devnet and must commit to the same `sha256(preimage)`.

When the treasury is unfunded there is no signature to confirm, so the script skips the positive assertion and instead checks that the empty request is refused cleanly.

To make this a real 200: fund the treasury (`POST /api/solana/fund` or the faucet link), then re-run from the Challenge request.

item.name: 04 · Payout Rails
item.description:
Both rails share the ledger reservation, the threshold and the 70/30 rule. Only the settlement call differs.

These requests accept **200** (paid) or **409** (`THRESHOLD_NOT_REACHED`) because the ledger is stateful and the outcome depends on it, not on the request:

- A fresh reset starts the reader at €0.00. One settle credits €0.70 (a €1.00 impression at the 70% share), which is far above the €0.005 threshold shipped in `server/.env.example`, so it pays out on its own.
- `PAYPAL_AUTO_PAYOUT=true` fires **900ms** after a settlement crosses the threshold. By the time you click a payout button by hand, the credit has usually already been spent automatically, so a 409 means "already paid", not "broken".

Because both outcomes are legitimate, the tests assert the response *shape* in either branch. To force a 200 by hand: switch `PAYPAL_AUTO_PAYOUT=false`, reset, settle once, then call payout.

Executes the 70/30 split as a single devnet transaction: two transfers plus a memo committing to the payout reference and the L402 hash.

One transaction means both legs succeed or neither does. Amounts are integer base units, so the split cannot drift.

item.name: 05 · PayPal Webhooks
item.description:
Inbound notifications from PayPal. These are the only endpoints in the collection that a *client* never calls — PayPal does.

The contract is unusual, so the tests assert it explicitly: a well-formed event that changes nothing must still answer **200**, because PayPal retries every non-2xx forever. The `outcome` field distinguishes `handled` (ledger updated) from `ignored`, `duplicate` and `unmatched`.

No signature headers are sent here. With `PAYPAL_WEBHOOK_ID` unset the route reports `signature: "skipped"` rather than pretending to verify — the same honesty the validator relies on. Set that variable (and `PAYPAL_WEBHOOK_STRICT=true` to refuse unverified events) to exercise the real round-trip.

exec: pm.test('200 acknowledged, or 401 when verification is configured', () => {
pm.test('an accepted receipt names the event and an outcome', () => {
// PAYPAL_WEBHOOK_ID is configured, so an unsigned request is refused.
// That is the endpoint working: PayPal always signs its notifications.
pm.test('an unverifiable signature is reported, not assumed', () => {
pm.test('the rail is the PayPal one and the ledger is intact', () => {

request.description: A payout item success notification. The batch id is deliberately not in the ledger, so a fresh run answers `outcome: "unmatched"` — acknowledged, nothing changed. That is the delivery-and-acknowledge contract working, not a failure. Re-posting the same event id inside a run answers `duplicate`; `POST /api/dev/reset` clears the replay guard so this request stays repeatable.

item.name: 99 · Maintenance (destructive)
item.description: Resets the simulator so the suite is repeatable. Left last and clearly labelled because it clears live state.

request.description:
**Destructive.** Clears balances, campaign budgets, L402 contexts, payout history and the Solana replay guard.

Remove this request from a run when you are demoing against a ledger you want to keep.
